sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.text:
3 Methodology In this section, we first describe the overall model design for incorporating latent actions into VLMs (Sec. 3.1 ). Next, we detail the unsupervised construction of the latent action space (Sec. 3.2 ). Finally, we introduce the procedure of latent action based RL fine-tuning (Sec. 3.3 ). 3.1 Model Design To fine-tune MCAs via latent action RL, we introduce three new modules, as illustrated in Figure 1 . These modules are designed to share a base VLM while adding a small number of additional parameters, thereby introducing only marginal computational overhead. For further details on the model design, please refer to the Appendix A . Language World Model [LaTeX: f_{	ext{world}}] f world f_{	ext{world}} The language world model [LaTeX: f_{	ext{world}}(x^{T_{t+1}}|x^{V},x^{T_{1:t}},a_{t})] f world ( x T t + 1 | x V , x T 1 : t , a t ) f_{	ext{world}}(x^{T_{t+1}}|x^{V},x^{T_{1:t}},a_{t}) takes current observations [LaTeX: (x^{V},x^{T_{1:t}})] ( x V , x T 1 : t ) (x^{V},x^{T_{1:t}}) and a latent action [LaTeX: a_{t}] a t a_{t} as input, and auto-regressively outputs the next token [LaTeX: x^{T_{t+1}}] x T t + 1 x^{T_{t+1}} . The latent action [LaTeX: a_{t}] a t a_{t} is provided by the inverse dynamics model [LaTeX: f_{	ext{inverse}}] f inverse f_{	ext{inverse}} during constructing the latent action space, and by the policy [LaTeX: \pi_{	heta}] π θ \pi_{	heta} during inference and RL phases. Inverse Dynamics Model [LaTeX: f_{	ext{inverse}}] f inverse f_{	ext{inverse}} The inverse dynamics model [LaTeX: f_{	ext{inverse}}(a_{t}|x^{V},x^{T_{1:t+1}})] f inverse ( a t | x V , x T 1 : t + 1 ) f_{	ext{inverse}}(a_{t}|x^{V},x^{T_{1:t+1}}) takes future observations [LaTeX: (x^{V},x^{T_{1:t+1}})] ( x V , x T 1 : t + 1 ) (x^{V},x^{T_{1:t+1}}) as input, and outputs a discrete latent action index [LaTeX: a_{t}\in\{1,\dots,|\mathcal{C}|\}] a t ∈ { 1 , … , | 𝒞 | } a_{t}\in\{1,\dots,|\mathcal{C}|\} for the current step. The corresponding latent action embedding [LaTeX: c_{a_{t}}=\mathcal{C}[a_{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d}] c a t = 𝒞 ⁡ [ a t ] ∈ ℝ d c_{a_{t}}=\mathcal{C}[a_{t}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is then retrieved from the trainable codebook [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{C}|	imes d}] 𝒞 ∈ ℝ | 𝒞 | × d \mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{C}|	imes d} and used by [LaTeX: f_{	ext{world}}] f world f_{	ext{world}} to reconstruct the next token [LaTeX: x^{T_{t+1}}] x T t + 1 x^{T_{t+1}} . Note that [LaTeX: f_{	ext{inverse}}] f inverse f_{	ext{inverse}} only assists training and does not serve for the inference phase. Policy Model [LaTeX: \pi_{	heta}] π θ \pi_{	heta} The latent action policy model [LaTeX: \pi_{	heta}(a_{t}|x^{V},x^{T_{1:t}})] π θ ( a t | x V , x T 1 : t ) \pi_{	heta}(a_{t}|x^{V},x^{T_{1:t}}) takes the current observations [LaTeX: (x^{V},x^{T_{1:t}})] ( x V , x T 1 : t ) (x^{V},x^{T_{1:t}}) as input, and predicts latent action [LaTeX: a_{t}] a t a_{t} for the current step. Since the language world model [LaTeX: f_{	ext{world}}] f world f_{	ext{world}} is controlled by latent actions, we can optimize the latent action distribution of [LaTeX: \pi_{	heta}] π θ \pi_{	heta} for steering [LaTeX: f_{	ext{world}}] f world f_{	ext{world}} to generate responses toward higher rewards. 3.2 Latent Action Space Learning Following Jia et al. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.text: 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Models We build the language world model, inverse dynamics model, and policy model upon the same foundation vision-language model. Specifically, we use Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct Bai et al. (2025b) for main experiments. The latent action space is implemented as a codebook with size [LaTeX: |\mathcal{C}|=128] | 𝒞 | = 128 |\mathcal{C}|=128 . Datasets During the latent action space construction stage (Section 3.2 ), we use a mixture of paired image-text corpora [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}^{VT}] 𝒟 V ​ T \mathcal{D}^{VT} and text-only corpora [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}^{T}] 𝒟 T \mathcal{D}^{T} . For [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}^{VT}] 𝒟 V ​ T \mathcal{D}^{VT} , we collect image-caption pairs from Conceptual-12M Changpinyo et al. (2021) , multimodal news articles from N24News Wang et al. (2022) , and multimodal Wikipedia data from WikiWeb2M Burns et al. (2023) , totaling 14 million images and 1 billion text tokens. For [LaTeX: \mathcal{D}^{T}] 𝒟 T \mathcal{D}^{T} , we collect text-only data mainly from the SlimPajama-627B dataset Soboleva et al. (2023) , which contains 627 billion text tokens. For latent action RL (Section 3.3 ), we evaluate our method on two downstream tasks: 1) multimodal role-playing conversation on MMRole Dai et al. (2025) , where we focus on the challenging Comment subset; we train on the in-distribution (ID) split and evaluate on ID and out-of-distribution (OOD) test sets; 2) multimodal personalized conversation on PCogAlignBench Li et al. (2025a) , where we train the agent on the LS1 set and evaluate on LS1 and LS2 test sets. Evaluation Metrics We adopt the LLM-as-a-Judge metric to evaluate model performance, using prompt templates validated by Dai et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) , which show high correlation with human judgments. For each sample, the LLM judge scores both the model and ground-truth responses across benchmark-specific dimensions, with scores ranging 1-10. Then, following Dai et al. (2025) , we report the ratio of the model’s average score to the ground-truth response’s average score across all evaluation dimensions. We report the mean and standard deviation across three evaluation runs. Please refer to the Appendix B for more experimental details. 4.2 Main Results Overall Performance Table 1 reports the experimental results of token-level baselines and our proposed latent action level RL. Based on these results, we have made the following observations. 1) Our method achieves superior performance across diverse tasks and datasets. On average, it outperforms token-level RL by 4% (averaged over all settings). 2) Our latent action framework is RL-agnostic and readily compatible with diverse policy optimization algorithms, including GRPO, Dr. GRPO, DAPO, and BNPO, yielding consistent gains over baselines. 3) The improvements brought by latent actions are consistently observed in both 3B and 7B models, demonstrating the scalability of our approach. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) , we assess eight dimensions on MMRole : 1) Instruction Adherence (IA), 2) Fluency (Flu), 3) Coherency (Coh), 4) Image-Text Relevance (ITR), 5) Response Accuracy (RA), 6) Personality Consistency (OC), 7) Knowledge Consistency (KC), and 8) Tone Consistency (TC). On PCogAlignBench , we evaluate: 1) Role-Set Awareness (RSA), 2) Body Behavior Awareness (BBA), 3) Mind Feelings Awareness (MFA), 4) Contextual Awareness (CA), and 5) Conversational Flow (CF). Best results are in bold . 4.3 Ablation Study To assess the contribution of main components in our method, we conduct ablation study using three variants. 1) Ours w/o cycle consistency : We remove the cycle consistency loss during cross-modal projector training, and instead directly apply the projector trained only on paired image-text data, i.e., removing [LaTeX: \mathcal{L}_{\text{cycle}}] ℒ cycle \mathcal{L}_{\text{cycle}} in Eq. 6 ; 2) Ours w/o cross-modal projector : We remove the cross-modal projector entirely, and learn the latent action codebook directly from text-only representations [LaTeX: e^{T}] e T e^{T} ; 3) Ours w/o text-only data : We construct the latent action space using only the limited paired multimodal corpus, excluding all text-only data. The results of ablation study are shown in Table 2 . From Table 2 , we can make the following observations. 1) Removing the cycle consistency loss leads to an average performance drop of 2.3%, indicating that fine-tuning the projector on large-scale text-only data via cycle consistency loss is crucial for improving its robustness. 2) Eliminating the cross-modal projector causes a noticeable decline in performance. This suggests that directly learning the latent action space from text-only embeddings may introduce a unimodal bias, i.e., the trained latent action policy model overly relies textual representations and fail to effectively handle multimodal scenarios. 3) Solely leveraging paired multimodal data results in the largest performance degradation, particularly in out-of-distribution settings (e.g., OOD on MMRole and LS2 on PCogAlignBench ). This highlights that the limited diversity and coverage of paired image-text corpora constrain the generalization capability of latent action policy models. 4.4 Analysis Rollout Diversity with Latent Actions Benefiting from the reduced action space, the constructed latent action space is expected to improve the agent’s rollout diversity during RL exploration, i.e., generating more diverse responses. Prior work has shown that such diversity is critical for improving the upper bound of RL performance Li et al. (2025b) ; Yu et al. (2025) . Following Jia et al. Computational Budget To assess the computational overhead introduced by our latent action framework, we analyze the time cost during RL training. Specifically, we consider the time cost in two stages: 1) Rollout : generating multiple candidate responses per prompt; 2) Policy update : updating the policy model using the computed rewards. We present the time cost per RL step of our method and the baseline in Fig. 5 , using GRPO as an example with a rollout batch size of 8. As illustrated in Fig. 5 , our latent action based method incurs a 1.13× slowdown in rollout time, due to the additional latent action prediction step. However, policy updates in latent action RL require only 0.86× the time of the baseline, as the optimization involves adjusting the policy’s output distribution over a compact latent action space, rather than the full token vocabulary. Overall, the total RL training time is only 1.08× that of token-level RL. Figure 5: Time cost per step during RL training, including rollout, policy update, and total time.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.text: Limitations We acknowledge the following limitations in our work. First, the additional latent action prediction step increases RL training time by 1.08× and inference latency by 1.13×. Second, due to constraints of computational resources, we evaluate our latent action based approach on multimodal conversational tasks, and leave validation on more tasks to future work, such as visual mathematical reasoning.

title: Controlling Multimodal Conversational Agents with Coverage-Enhanced Latent Actions
